description: Car Hacking Village focuses on automotive cybersecurity, in-vehicle network architectures (CAN, CAN FD, J1939), passive keyless entry exploits, EV charging stations, and ADAS sensor attacks.

talks.title: Bug Hunter's Guide to Bashing for Car Hacking Bug Bashes
talks.teaser: Jay Turla shares winning methodologies for automotive bug bashes, providing bug bounty hunters with hardware and firmware preparation blueprints.
talks.summary:
The Rise of Automotive Bug Bounty Programs

Automotive manufacturers and Tier-1 suppliers increasingly host dedicated automotive bug bashes and live hacking events to identify connected vehicle vulnerabilities.

Preparation and Tooling for Live Vehicle Hacking

Jay Turla outlines essential hardware tools (CAN adapters, SDRs, logic analyzers) and software frameworks needed to audit target vehicles.

Common High-Impact Automotive Vulnerabilities

Turla reviews recurring bugs discovered during live bashes—including insecure UDS diagnostic services, hardcoded telematics API keys, and unauthenticated CAN commands.

Actionable Advice for Bug Bounty Hunters

The author provides triage strategies, report writing templates, and tips to maximize bounty earnings in automotive programs.

talks.title: Build Automotive Gateways with Ease
talks.teaser: Don Hatfield explores central automotive gateways, explaining how multi-bus routing, translation, and security firewalls protect in-vehicle networks.
talks.summary:
The Evolution of In-Vehicle Network Topologies

Modern vehicles integrate dozens of Electronic Control Units (ECUs) communicating across divergent protocols—such as CAN, CAN FD, LIN, FlexRay, and Automotive Ethernet.

The Central Role of Automotive Gateways

Don Hatfield explains how automotive central gateways act as the nervous system, routing messages, translating frame formats, and isolating security domains.

Designing Secure and Flexible Gateway Hardware

Hatfield demonstrates building prototype automotive gateways using open hardware and modular embedded development platforms.

Implementing Diagnostic Firewalling and Filtering

The presentation details implementing stateful CAN frame filtering and rate limiting to prevent compromised infotainment units from injecting safety-critical commands.

talks.title: Commercial Transportation Trucking Hacking: J1939 & Trailer Networks
talks.teaser: Ben Gardiner breaks down heavy commercial vehicle hacking, analyzing J1939 tractor protocols, PLC4TRUCKS trailer networks, and fleet telematics.
talks.summary:
Introduction to Commercial Heavy Vehicle Networks

Commercial tractor-trailers and heavy transportation vehicles rely on distinct network architectures that differ significantly from passenger automobiles.

Deconstructing J1939, J1708, and J2497 Protocols

Ben Gardiner provides a deep dive into heavy vehicle protocols—including SAE J1939 250k CAN, legacy J1708/J1587 serial buses, and J2497 (PLC4TRUCKS) trailer power line signaling.

Exploiting Telematics and Electronic Logging Devices

Gardiner demonstrates attack vectors targeting mandatory Electronic Logging Devices (ELDs) and commercial fleet management transceivers.

Physical and Cyber Defenses for Freight Transportation

The author reviews security best practices for freight fleets, securing physical diagnostic ports, and implementing heavy-duty firewall modules.

talks.title: From CTF to CVE: Finding Flaws in Hyundai Blue Link Telematics
talks.teaser: Bill Hatzer shares how practicing mobile app proxying for a CTF uncovered an unauthenticated API vulnerability in Hyundai Blue Link telematics.
talks.summary:
Transitioning from CTF Challenges to Real-World Research

While participating in defensive and offensive CTFs, practicing foundational techniques often leads researchers to discover real-world zero-day vulnerabilities.

Intercepting Mobile Telematics Traffic with Burp Suite

Bill Hatzer details setting up a mobile testing lab, bypassing certificate pinning on an Android phone, and intercepting Hyundai Blue Link API traffic.

Discovering the Telematics API Authorization Bypass

Hatzer demonstrates how flawed backend API endpoint validation allowed an attacker to query vehicle status and send remote telematics commands without valid session tokens.

Coordinated Disclosure and Vendor Remediation

The author reviews the coordinated disclosure timeline with Hyundai and provides developers with mobile API authentication hardening guidelines.

talks.title: Fuzzing CAN & CAN FD ECUs and Networks
talks.teaser: Samir Bhagwat delivers an overview of automated fuzzing techniques for CAN and CAN FD electronic control units and in-vehicle networks.
talks.summary:
This DEF CON talk covers fuzzing can & can fd ecus and networks.

talks.title: Keynote: Ready, Fire, Aim - Hacking State and Federal Law Enforcement Vehicles
talks.teaser: Keynote speaker Alissa Knight exposes vulnerabilities in connected law enforcement vehicle telematics, enabling remote vehicle unlocking and siren hijacking.
talks.summary:
The Connected Fleet in Law Enforcement and Public Safety

Modern police interceptors and federal law enforcement vehicles are equipped with sophisticated connected telematics, automated license plate readers, and remote dispatch consoles.

Reverse Engineering Law Enforcement Fleet Telematics APIs

Alissa Knight investigates mobile applications and cloud APIs used by law enforcement agencies, uncovering broken object level authorization (BOLA) flaws.

Demonstrating Remote Vehicle Takeover Vectors

Knight demonstrates how an attacker could track real-time patrol car locations, unlock doors, start engines, and hijack lightbars and sirens across hundreds of active police cruisers.

Hardening Emergency Vehicle Fleet Infrastructure

The keynote calls for rigorous third-party penetration testing, strict API gateway authentication, and isolated networks for emergency responder fleets.

talks.title: Compromising the Tesla Model X Keyless Entry System
talks.teaser: KU Leuven researcher Lennert Wouters reverse engineers the Tesla Model X BLE key fob and pairing protocol, unlocking and driving away the car in minutes.
talks.summary:
The Architecture of the Tesla Model X Keyless Entry

The Tesla Model X utilizes Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) key fobs to communicate with the vehicle Body Control Module (BCM) for hands-free passive entry.

Reverse Engineering the Key Fob Firmware and BLE Protocols

Lennert Wouters extracts and reverse engineers the key fob firmware, discovering an unauthenticated firmware update mechanism over the BLE link.

Crafting the Relay and Key Extraction Attack

Using an inexpensive Raspberry Pi and CAN diagnostic tool, Wouters pushes rogue firmware to the fob via BLE, extracts cryptographic unlock keys, and drives off.

Over-the-Air Patching and Hardware Security Modules

The presentation details Tesla's coordinated response, including over-the-air firmware updates that enforced cryptographic signing on key fob updates.

talks.title: Marco: Vehicle Identification & Tracking via Passive Keyless Entry
talks.teaser: Nick Ashworth presents 'Marco', a radar-like RF attack that probes Passive Keyless Entry (PKE) systems to identify and track specific vehicles across a city.
talks.summary:
Beyond Relay Theft: Exploiting PKE for Surveillance

While research on Passive Keyless Entry (PKE) focuses on relay attacks for vehicle theft, the unencrypted challenge-response protocol introduces massive surveillance vulnerabilities.

Introducing the 'Marco' Vehicle Tracking Attack

Nick Ashworth presents 'Marco', an attack methodology that functions like cooperative radar by broadcasting low-frequency wakeup beacons.

Fingerprinting Unique Vehicle Cryptographic Responses

By measuring precise RF timing and response identifiers from a target vehicle's keyless transceivers, an attacker tracks specific cars without physical contact.

Mitigating RF Tracking and Privacy Leaks in Connected Cars

The author discusses protocol enhancements, randomized transponder MAC addresses, and cryptographic challenges to prevent vehicle stalking.

talks.title: Remote Adversarial Phantom Attacks on Tesla & Mobileye ADAS
talks.teaser: Ben Nassi demonstrates 'split-second phantom attacks', projecting fleeting images onto roads to trick Tesla Autopilot and Mobileye into sudden phantom braking.
talks.summary:
The Brittleness of Advanced Driver-Assistance Systems (ADAS)

Commercial ADAS platforms rely on camera feeds and computer vision neural networks to detect road obstacles, lane markings, and traffic signs in real time.

Discovering Split-Second Phantom Attacks

Ben Nassi reveals that projecting depthless images (such as a projected stop sign or pedestrian) for a few milliseconds causes Tesla Autopilot and Mobileye to register real obstacles.

Demonstrating Remote Phantom Braking on Active Vehicles

Nassi showcases live field tests where projected phantom images or hijacked digital road signs caused moving vehicles to execute dangerous emergency phantom braking.

Designing Resilient Sensor Fusion for Autonomous Vehicles

The author discusses mitigating phantom attacks through multi-sensor verification (LiDAR, radar) and temporal consistency filtering in perception models.

talks.title: Remotely Rooting Electric Vehicle Charging Stations
talks.teaser: Huajiang Chen and Wu Ming present remote root exploits (CVE-2021-22707, CVE-2021-22708) in Schneider Electric commercial EV charging stations.
talks.summary:
The Expanding Threat Surface of EV Charging Infrastructure

As electric vehicles proliferate globally, connected Electric Vehicle Supply Equipment (EVSE) charging stations represent critical, internet-connected electrical grid infrastructure.

Security Audit of Schneider Electric EV Charging Stations

Huajiang Chen and Wu Ming dissect Schneider Electric commercial EV chargers, auditing embedded firmware, Linux operating systems, and management interfaces.

Chaining 3 Zero-Days for Unauthenticated Remote Root

The researchers uncover multiple vulnerabilities—including hardcoded credentials, unauthenticated web administration portals, and command injection via OCPP protocols.

Impact on the Power Grid and Charging Security Standards

The authors demonstrate how compromised chargers could be weaponized into botnets to disrupt regional power grids, concluding with vendor remediation patches.

talks.title: Safety 3rd: Defeating Chevy StabiliTrak for Electric Vehicle Track Racing
talks.teaser: Eric Gershman reverse engineers Chevy Bolt and Spark EV CAN buses to defeat StabiliTrak Electronic Stability Control, unlocking full track racing performance.
talks.summary:
The Challenge of Electronic Stability Control in Track Racing

Modern electric vehicles enforce rigid Electronic Stability Control (ESC / StabiliTrak) systems that cut electric motor torque and apply brakes when tires slip on a race track.

Reverse Engineering the Chevy Bolt and Spark EV CAN Buses

Eric Gershman captures and analyzes in-vehicle CAN bus traffic between the brake control module, steering angle sensor, and motor inverter.

Designing the CAN Interceptor and Spoofing Hardware

Gershman builds a custom microcontroller CAN bridge that intercepts yaw rate and wheel speed messages, spoofing stable telemetry to disable ESC interventions.

Dyno and Track Testing Results

The presentation showcases track testing results, proving full driver throttle control and demonstrating safe automotive hardware modification practices.
